Our baseline model consists of a few convolutional layers followed by a fully connected layer. We train this model on ImageNet and achieve state-of-the-art results on the benchmark tasks. constructed_args.summary: We introduce a novel deep residual learning framework for image recognition.  Our key innovation is the design of deep residual blocks, which allow us to train very deep networks (up to 152 layers) without suffering from degradation problems. Residual blocks have two key functions: firstly, they allow gradient to flow more easily through the network during training, and secondly, they enable the network to learn more complex representations by stacking multiple residual blocks. We demonstrate that deep residual networks achieve state-of-the-art results on benchmark image classification tasks, surpassing previous methods by a significant margin. We also analyze the effectiveness of different residual block architectures and training strategies.
constructed_args.title: Deep Residual Learning for Image Recognition

constructed_args.summary: Language models are generally trained by predicting the next word in a sequence. This works well for tasks like text generation, but struggles with tasks requiring reasoning or understanding of context. We introduce GPT-3, a large language model with 175 billion parameters, trained on a massive dataset of text and code. GPT-3 exhibits few-shot learning abilities, achieving state-of-the-art performance on a variety of tasks with only a few examples. It can translate languages, write different kinds of creative content, and answer your questions in an informative way, even if they are open ended, challenging, or strange. We explore the capabilities and limitations of GPT-3, and discuss the broader implications of large language models for artificial intelligence.
constructed_args.title: Large Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners
